entries.text: On a device that turns out to be too slow to build the brain's 3D shapes in reasonable time, the remaining structures are now built at reduced detail so the page still opens promptly, and the loading screen says so rather than quietly serving you a coarser brain. Only the shapes soften; no data changes

The startup progress bar now reflects the real remaining work: it advances while a single structure is being built rather than only once it lands, and it weighs each structure by how much work it actually costs, so a long pause reads as progress instead of a freeze

The startup progress bar is now finer-grained: it advances while a single brain structure is being built (not only once the whole structure lands) and the caption counts them off, "Building Hippocampus… (12/46)", so a slow phone reads as making progress instead of looking frozen. The "Loading shapes" step counts too
The Data browser now scrolls sideways when it is narrower than its four columns, so a node's name, notion and kind stay on one readable line instead of being squeezed into a few letters per column
Opening the Data browser now gives it the whole window instead of a sliver beside the brain, so its four columns have room to be read

The Data browser is laid out as a real table: the column titles sit exactly over the cells they name, thin rules separate the columns, and every other line is shaded so the eye follows one node all the way across
The scene pane is now called "3D Controls", which says what it drives
Hiding the brain while the panel was folded down left an empty window; it now unfolds the panel to fill the screen
The downloadable data files opened in a tab instead of being downloaded as an unknown file type
The cannabinoid is listed under its full name, Tetrahydrocannabinol; searching THC still finds it

The address bar now describes the whole view, so a link brings someone to exactly what you were looking at: every open tab and the order you dragged them into, which one is in front, the popup you had up, the sliders and toggles, the open section, what you had typed in search, and roughly where the brain is turned. Copy the URL, that is the link
A link to a pathway (`#focusConnection=...`) opened nothing; it now opens the pathway it names
A link asking for the 3D brain to be shown (`#panel=0`) was ignored for a visitor who had previously turned the brain off; the link now wins
In French, the release notes printed each entry's commit codes twice; they now appear once, as links

Four more cannabinoids join THC in the Drugs list: cannabidiol (CBD), cannabinol (CBN), nabilone (the antiemetic) and rimonabant (the withdrawn anti-obesity drug), each with what it does at CB1 and, where a lab measured it, its binding strength
Fifty-one drug actions that were already in the dataset but showed no source now carry the Guide to Pharmacology entry that states them, so a green check replaces the red cross
The Data browser now opens as its own tab instead of a dropdown inside the panel, so the whole list of facts gets the full pane

Two more things are now shareable as a link: the Data browser itself (add `#browser=1` to the address) and the reading mode that hides the 3D brain (`#panel=1`, or `#panel=0` to force the brain back on)
The Data browser explains what a node is and labels its columns with the fields each line carries, so it reads as the graph of facts it is
A "The same data as files" link at the top of the Data browser opens the list of downloadable data files

A sourcing badge in the Data browser only offered "Click for details"; it now shows the actual source behind the fact (the quote, the measured affinity, or the reasons to doubt it), like the same badge inside a panel
"Show both hemispheres" is now off by default in the Data browser, so each region is read once instead of twice, and the checkbox only appears when brain structures are actually in view

The Data browser now lists both hemispheres of a region, so its counts line up with the sourcing statistics, and a new "Show both hemispheres" checkbox collapses each left/right pair back to a single line for reading
Hovering an active-metabolite bullet in the Drugs list now brightens its text as intended (the hover colour pointed at an undefined style token, so nothing happened)
Applied a backlog of measured binding affinities across 26 drugs (melperone gains its whole measured table); measured-affinity coverage of drug bindings rises from 87% to 88%

A new "Data browser" section lists every fact in the dataset in one searchable list, filterable by type and by how well sourced it is, and each line jumps to the panel that explains it. It pairs nicely with the hide-3D button for full-screen browsing
A new button at the top of the panel hides the 3D brain so the panel can use the whole screen for reading. Press it again to bring the brain back, and your choice is remembered for next time

Added domperidone, the first drug of a new "Antiemetic / prokinetic" class, with measured D2 and D3 affinities, its metabolism route and its molecule drawing. Its notes flag that it barely crosses the blood-brain barrier
Molecule drawings can be fetched again from Wikipedia (their image links recently changed shape and the importer no longer recognized them)
Separating and reassembling the brain is much smoother: the arrows now reshape themselves in place instead of being rebuilt from scratch on every single frame, which is what made the motion stutter

The opening animation is now two moves instead of one: the view turns around the blown-apart brain first, pauses a beat, then the regions glide back together. Doing both at once was more than a modest graphics card could draw smoothly
The author byline on the loading screen now sits between the title and the tagline instead of in a corner
The opening animation waits a second before it starts and now unfolds twice as slowly, so the brain assembles smoothly instead of stuttering on the first frames
The "What's new" popup's own title and each version heading in it are bigger, so the notes are legible at a glance instead of reading like the small print
Receptors and other drug targets now link to ClinPGx, the pharmacogenomics database: which variants of the gene behind them change how a drug works on you

The gene and protein databases (ClinPGx, UniProt) are now searched by gene symbol rather than by the receptor's display name, so a receptor written with a Greek letter (α1A) actually lands on its entry (ADRA1A) instead of an empty result page
Every drug now links to ClinPGx, the pharmacogenomics database: which gene variants change how you respond to it. The external links run EMA, FDA, ClinPGx, then Drugs.com
The Metabolism section gains a "Pathways" link: the rows below say which enzyme handles the drug, ClinPGx draws the whole route
An enzyme's own panel links to its ClinPGx page, where the poor- versus ultra-rapid-metabolizer variants and the dosing guidance live
The version number was missing from the panel header and the loading screen for the last two releases, and the "What's new" popup could not tell you anything had shipped

A brain structure's panel now lists the receptors and other drug targets found there, grouped by neurotransmitter system: the question "what sits in the hippocampus?" was only answerable from each receptor's own page before
Every row carries that region's own source grade, the same claim the receptor's own panel shows from the other end, so the two ends can never disagree
A receptor present throughout the brain is listed in every region, tagged as such, so it does not read as a claim about that region in particular
The About popup now offers the tutorial before it warns about the drug animations, and the button reads "Start the tutorial"

The animation legend is shorter and better ordered: the two bullets that stated the obvious are gone, the gem dots say where they appear, and the beads are explained before the glow that refers back to them
Two links say what they do: the data dropdown reads "Click to access the structured data", and the feedback link names GitHub

A pathway the book only states as a sweep ("these neurons project to virtually every part of the neuraxis") now wears the orange "uncertain" badge instead of a green check: the sentence is real and quoted, but it names none of the regions we drew the arrows to, and the badge says so

35 of the 95 pathways are concerned, mostly the diffuse ascending systems (histamine, serotonin, noradrenaline, acetylcholine to the cortex, and the striatal splits). A pathway whose source does name its target, such as the raphe to the thalamus, keeps its green check
The overall sourcing figure does not move: an "uncertain" claim still rests on a real quoted document, so it stays counted as backed and only leaves the green tally

Histamine now reaches every region that carries a histamine receptor: fourteen new pathways take the tuberomammillary nucleus to three more lobes, the cingulate cortex, the hippocampus, the amygdala, the striatum, the olfactory bulb, the brainstem and the cerebellum
A sedating antihistamine (diphenhydramine, mirtazapine, quetiapine and every drowsy antipsychotic) now shows a real histaminergic fan instead of lighting receptors with no supply drawn near them
Histamine is the first transmitter system in neurarium with complete coverage: every region that expresses it is reached

The About popup no longer explains the animations as one dense paragraph: it is now a collapsed "What the animations mean" list, one bullet per thing you can actually see (the dimmed brain, the coloured dots, the glow, the streaming beads, the sequential circuit pulse, the selection rim, a dotted arrow), each opening with what it is and then developing it
The warning that the drug animations are the least scientific part of neurarium now sits outside that dropdown, so it is read rather than hidden behind a click
Two things the popup never said: what a dotted arrow means, and why the metabolism and interaction sections light nothing in the 3D scene
"Take a tour" is now "See the tutorial"

Serotonin and noradrenaline now reach where their receptors are: fifteen new pathways take the raphe nuclei to the thalamus, three more lobes, the cingulate cortex, the striatum and the substantia nigra, and the locus coeruleus to three more lobes, the cingulate cortex, the hypothalamus and the cerebellum
Focusing an antidepressant now shows a real serotonergic fan across the brain instead of four lonely arrows
The thalamus gets its acetylcholine supply: the mesopontine cholinergic neurons of the pons, the other half of the brain's cholinergic map

The pineal gland joins the brain, along with melatonin as a system of its own: the MT1 and MT2 receptors finally have a source for the hormone they respond to. It is drawn as a hormonal route to the body clock, not as a nerve tract
Every one of these claims is quote-checked against Kandel's Principles of Neural Science or the Nieuwenhuys atlas

The nucleus basalis of Meynert joins the brain: the basal-forebrain nucleus that supplies the whole cortex with acetylcholine, with its six projections to the four lobes, the cingulate cortex and the amygdala

An anticholinergic drug (scopolamine, an antipsychotic with muscarinic blockade) now has a cholinergic pathway to travel: until now it lit up cortical receptors with no acetylcholine supply drawn anywhere near them
A region named after a person keeps that name capitalized when the side is added ("Right nucleus basalis of Meynert")
A source's tooltip now shows where in the book the passage sits, as a trail like "Clozapine › Side effects › How Drug Causes Side Effects", for all five books
The uncertain claims were missing from the per-topic bars in the Sources popup, which left a gap in each bar and understated its percentage
"What's new" no longer skips a visit where you grabbed the separate slider while the brain was assembling
A release whose notes had not been published yet is no longer marked as read, which used to lose it for good
22 more drug bindings carry the uncertain badge: where the book names a whole receptor family and we publish its subtypes, a subtype with no measured affinity is our own reading, not the book's
The uncertain badge is now derived from where each quote sits in the book rather than from a hand-written list, so a new drug is covered the day it lands
A new orange "uncertain" badge takes the green check's place on a claim whose quote does not actually say it is about that drug; hover it for the reasons to doubt it, each with its own source
When the guided tour needs to scroll a panel, a purple arrow now shows which way it is going and lands on what it is taking you to
A metabolite that has its own page now offers a "see its bindings" button instead of showing nothing
Switching between detail tabs keeps where you were reading in each one
In the drugs list, a metabolite that itself has metabolites now shows them indented under it

89 drug bindings, almost all the tricyclics' antihistamine, anticholinergic and alpha-1 side-effect claims, now carry the uncertain badge: the book states them as a rule without naming the drug, and half are backed by a measured affinity anyway
This "What's new" popup: after an update it lists everything that changed since your last visit, and you can reopen it any time from About
Every release is dated, and one button under the new ones opens the whole history, back to the release that added drug half-lives and metabolites
A drug's possible interactions now say the direction once, as a heading, and read "could raise" rather than "raises": they are a flag to check with a prescriber, never a verdict
The guided tour now walks through a drug's metabolism and interactions too
Twenty book quotes were cut mid-sentence and lost the subject they were about; they now read as whole sentences
Every quote is now checked to come from the right drug's own pages in the book, not a neighbour's
Five metabolism facts that a too-strict filter had been silently dropping are back, including alcohol's own enzyme
NKCC1 and bumetanide, the pair behind the chloride gradient that decides whether GABA calms or excites a neuron
Molecule diagrams for the seven newest drugs
Search now finds a drug by its other names, so "Prozac" and "fluox" both land on fluoxetine
Alcohol's action on the NMDA receptor is now sourced rather than assumed
Alcohol, which was missing from the drug list
Reserpine, the drug that empties the monoamine storage vesicles
The Parkinson's dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors: pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine, rasagiline and friends
Molecule diagrams for nine more drugs
Removed 91 drug-receptor links that came from a Stahl sentence describing the drug class, not the drug
Furosemide, a diuretic that also damps one specific GABA-A receptor in the cerebellum
Methamphetamine now shows its sigma-1 action alongside its dopamine one
The amphetamines now empty the neurotransmitter storage vesicles in the animation, which is how they really raise dopamine
Reloading the site is much faster on a phone: the code is now checked for updates instead of downloaded again every time
21 of the 33 drug actions that carried no source at all now have one, quote-checked against the book it came from
Each active metabolite now says which enzyme forms it, where a source states it: 14 of the 36 so far, the rest openly marked as unsourced
The drugs outside the reference prescriber's guide now have their metabolism sourced too, read from their encyclopedia articles
The alpha-2 receptor's role in setting noradrenaline tone is now backed by a textbook quote
The tuberomammillary nucleus got its encyclopedia link, so its panel now shows a description
What kind of receptor something is, and whether it excites or inhibits, is now backed by the Guide to Pharmacology rather than asserted
Where that source and this dataset disagree, the disagreement is reported rather than quietly overwritten
Refreshed the survey of what is still unsourced against the live figures
Possible interactions can now be read two ways, by the other drug or by the enzyme they meet at, and clicking one lands you on the reason rather than the top of the page
The Enzymes section now looks like a section of its own, instead of an item tucked inside Drugs
Metabolism: each drug now lists the liver enzymes that clear it, or whose activity it changes, with the source for each
Possible drug interactions, worked out from those enzymes: which other drugs in the dataset could see their levels rise or fall
An Enzymes section in the side panel: pick an enzyme to see the drugs it handles, grouped by role
Molecule diagrams for the 53 drugs added in the previous release
Surveyed how drug metabolism could be sourced before building it
54 more marketed drugs, the ones the survey found missing, each with its sourced brand names and measured affinities
Two more benzodiazepines: bromazepam and clotiazepam
A region carrying many of a drug's targets no longer washes out to flat white; it now glows once, as brightly as the drug's strongest action there
Surveyed which marketed drugs the reference rosters have and this dataset does not
Bindings that only had a measured strength, with no known direction, now have one and light up the 3D scene like any other
The guided tour says up front that it takes about three minutes
The version number now also shows on the loading screen
The glowing dots on a region no longer vanish when you rotate the brain past a certain angle
A twelfth source, the Guide to Pharmacology's curated affinities, fills the targets a radioligand panel cannot reach: the benzodiazepine site, MAO, acetylcholinesterase, orexin, melatonin
It filled in 35 missing affinity values and 193 missing directions, taking measured-affinity coverage to 86%
"Found in" now answers how much, not only where: each region gets a bar showing the relative amount of that receptor, measured from human donor brains
Each profile says how many donors it rests on and how well they agreed; a gene whose donors disagreed publishes nothing rather than a shaky number
Metabolites now draw on the measured-affinity database directly, so one like norfluoxetine shows its eleven measured targets even though its own encyclopedia page lists none
Wrote up where receptor density and blood-brain-barrier data could come from, for a later pass
The "Sources & provenance" panel now opens one bar at a time: click the overall figure for a breakdown by kind of fact, then a kind for its grades and a real example you can jump to
Half-lives, metabolites and their receptor actions each got their own coverage bar in that panel
A metabolite's own receptor actions are now listed under it in the drug panel, not only on the receptor's side
Jumping from a receptor to a metabolite now flashes the right row, so you can see which of the drug's metabolites you landed on
Active metabolites now have receptor actions of their own, so a receptor's page lists them beside the drugs, marked "metabolite of"
Searching for a metabolite by name now finds it, and keeps the drug it comes from visible in the list
A metabolite made by two different drugs is now counted and listed once instead of twice
How long a drug stays in the body: each drug now shows its half-life, next to its brand names
Active metabolites: the substances your body turns a drug into that keep working on their own, each with its own half-life
A switch in the drug list to show or hide those metabolites under their parent drug
The new half-life and metabolite facts are counted in the sourcing tally like everything else, so the "% sourced" figure stays honest
